content:
**Quick answer:** Osteoarthritis involves structural changes and damage within a joint. Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune condition in which the immune system mistakenly attacks the lining of the joints, causing inflammation that can also affect other parts of the body. Both can cause pain, stiffness and swelling, so symptoms alone cannot always tell them apart.

## The two conditions at a glance

Because the symptoms overlap, it is not always possible to tell osteoarthritis (OA) and rheumatoid arthritis (RA) apart without an assessment. These are the general patterns, not rules: individual experiences vary, and diagnosis belongs with an appropriate healthcare professional.

*Osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis compared*

|  | Osteoarthritis | Rheumatoid arthritis |
|---|---|---|
| **Type** | Joint condition involving structural changes | Autoimmune inflammatory disease |
| **Common joints** | Knees, hips and small hand joints | Often hands, feet and wrists |
| **Pattern** | May affect individual joints differently | Often affects both sides, but not always |
| **Morning stiffness** | Often absent or shorter-lasting | Often more prolonged |
| **Whole-body symptoms** | Mainly joint-related | Can include fatigue and other symptoms |

## What is osteoarthritis?

Osteoarthritis is the most common type of arthritis. In a healthy joint, cartilage covers the ends of the bones and keeps movement smooth. In osteoarthritis, that cartilage can break down and other changes can develop in and around the joint. It most often affects the knees, hips and small joints of the hands.

Symptoms can include pain, stiffness, tenderness, swelling, difficulty moving the joint, and grating or crackling sensations during movement. How it feels varies considerably from person to person.

You may hear osteoarthritis described as "wear and tear", but that is too simplistic. Age is one factor, and previous joint injury, family history and body weight can all contribute. A diagnosis does not mean a joint is simply used up.

## What is rheumatoid arthritis?

Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune condition. The immune system mistakenly attacks the cells lining the joints, causing inflammation. It often affects the hands, feet and wrists, and because it is a systemic condition it can also cause tiredness, reduced energy and, in some people, inflammation in other parts of the body.

It often affects similar joints on both sides of the body, but that pattern is not universal. The exact trigger for the immune response is not fully understood; it is not caused by joint wear.

> **Why early assessment matters**
>
> Prompt assessment and treatment of suspected rheumatoid arthritis can help reduce the risk of worsening disease and joint damage.

## How are they diagnosed?

A GP will usually ask about your symptoms and examine the affected joints. In a typical presentation, osteoarthritis is often diagnosed clinically, so imaging is not always needed. Tests may be appropriate when another explanation for your symptoms is being considered.

Rheumatoid arthritis can be more complicated to diagnose, because several conditions cause joint inflammation and stiffness and no single blood test can prove or rule it out. Assessment may include a joint examination, blood tests and imaging, and suspected RA usually means referral to a rheumatology specialist.

## Is treatment different?

For osteoarthritis, management may include tailored therapeutic exercise, strengthening, general physical activity, weight management where appropriate, strategies that make daily activities easier, medicines when appropriate, physiotherapy and, for some people, surgery.

For rheumatoid arthritis, treatment focuses on controlling the autoimmune inflammation and reducing the risk of joint damage. This usually involves disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (DMARDs) alongside other medicines and supportive treatments. Do not start, stop or change arthritis medication without discussing it with the healthcare professional responsible for your treatment.

Appropriate physical activity can help in both conditions. The type and amount should reflect which joints are affected, your pain, swelling, strength, fatigue and current disease activity. Start gently, adapt to your ability, and stop if pain feels sharp, severe or unusual.

## When to speak to your GP

Arrange an appointment if you have unexplained joint pain, swelling or stiffness that does not settle. Assessment is particularly important for persistently swollen joints, prolonged morning stiffness, symptoms in several joints, similar symptoms in both hands or feet, worsening mobility, or persistent fatigue alongside joint symptoms.

> **When joint pain is urgent**
>
> Seek urgent medical advice for severe pain and swelling in a joint that starts suddenly, or if the skin around a painful joint is hot or red, or joint symptoms come with a high or low temperature or feeling hot, cold or shivery. Call 999 for a medical emergency such as severe breathing difficulty, chest pain or sudden weakness.

## Key takeaways

- Osteoarthritis involves structural changes within a joint; rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune inflammatory disease.
- RA can cause symptoms beyond the joints and often needs early specialist treatment.
- Symptoms overlap, so you cannot reliably diagnose yourself from pain alone.
- The two conditions can coexist, so do not assume every new symptom is caused by an existing diagnosis.
- Persistent or unexplained joint pain, swelling or stiffness should be assessed by your GP.

## Frequently asked questions

### Which is worse, osteoarthritis or rheumatoid arthritis?

It is not helpful to rank one as universally worse. Either condition can significantly affect quality of life, and severity varies between individuals.

### Does rheumatoid arthritis hurt all day?

Symptoms vary. Pain and stiffness change over time, and many people experience periods when symptoms become worse, often called flares.

### Can rheumatoid arthritis affect more than the joints?

Yes. RA is a systemic condition and can cause fatigue and, in some people, inflammation in other parts of the body.

### Is there a cure for osteoarthritis or rheumatoid arthritis?

Neither condition currently has a cure, but treatments and self-management approaches can help manage symptoms and function.

## A gentle next step

Understanding the difference can make joint symptoms feel less confusing, but you do not need to work out the diagnosis yourself. If you have persistent pain, swelling or stiffness, particularly prolonged morning stiffness or swelling in several joints, speak to your GP. You can also explore practical arthritis information and support from Living With Arthritis.
